title: Premonition
visual: Title 'Premonition v2'. A friendly laptop with a small glowing brain inside. Then a day/night split: sun side 'day: chats, thinking, trying', moon side 'night: sleep and practice'. Four status counters appear: 6 Adopted, 6 Testing, 3 Refuted, 1 Parked.
lines: Hi Ben. This is a tour of everything we've built into premonition.
The goal is simple: a personal assistant that lives on your laptop, and gets a little smarter every night.
We've tried sixteen ideas so far. Six are in. Six are still being tested. Three didn't work. And one is on the shelf.
Here's what each one does, and how it scored.

title: How to read the scores
visual: Three colored bars side by side with labels: grey 'stand-in (older small models)', teal 'K2-3.7B (small laptops)', violet 'Qwen3.6-35B (big laptops)'. A red dashed vertical line labelled 'pass mark, set before the test'.
lines: First, a quick key.
Grey bars come from small stand-in models we use to try ideas cheaply.
Teal is K2, the small brain for small laptops. Purple is Qwen, the big brain for big laptops.
And the red dashed line is the pass mark. We always set it before the test, so we can't fool ourselves.

title: Sleep
visual: Five-step strip: 1 pick facts said on 2+ days, 2 write practice questions, 3 check answers against the diary, 4 practice into a small add-on, 5 morning check. Then bars 'Remembers repeated facts, notes removed': stand-in 91.5 (grey), K2 96.5 (teal), Qwen3.6 96.0 (violet), pass line 75.
lines: Sleep is the heart of it.
Every night, the model picks out the things you keep mentioning, writes itself flashcards, checks them against its diary, and practices.
In the morning, a quick check undoes any night that made it worse.
The result? With its notes taken away, it still remembers about ninety-six out of a hundred repeated facts. On both real brains. The pass mark was seventy-five.
And it didn't get any dumber at everything else.

title: Two-step memory
visual: Chain: 'Sam's sister is Ana' + 'Ana lives in Oslo' -> 'Where does Sam's sister live? Oslo'. Bars two-step right: Qwen3.6 67.9 (violet), stand-in 38.5 (grey), K2 3.8 (teal, with a small 'bug' label). Goal line 95.
lines: Harder are questions that chain two facts together. Like, where does Sam's sister live?
Qwen gets about sixty-eight percent. The goal is ninety-five.
K2 scored almost zero, but that's a bug. It wasn't writing its practice questions in the right format. The fix is queued.

title: Longer nights
visual: A moon over a staircase of bars (grey): 1x work 53, 2x 67.5, 4x 76. Then a dashed outline bar '12 hours while Ben sleeps' labelled 'not tested yet'.
lines: More practice per night helps a lot.
Doubling the night's work took recall from fifty-three to sixty-seven. Four times took it to seventy-six. Now four times is the standard.
Next, we want to use the whole twelve hours you're asleep. That hasn't been tested yet.

title: Sleeping on 4-bit
visual: A smooth color gradient next to a 16-step blocky gradient labelled 'squeezed to 4-bit to fit a laptop'. Bars: K2 full quality 96.5, K2 squeezed 86.0 (teal), pass line 91.5. Qwen3.6 squeezed 96.0 (violet), pass 75.
lines: To fit on a laptop, the model gets squeezed, like saving a photo at low quality.
Can it still learn while squeezed? For K2, not well. It dropped from ninety-six to eighty-six, and failed.
So the small brain will sleep on a full-quality copy, then get squeezed again each morning. The big Qwen brain, oddly, did fine squeezed.

title: Whole-model sleep
visual: A grid of 100 dots where 2 flip color, labelled 'about 2 in 100 rounded values flip'. Bar 'share of the gain kept after squeezing' 94 (grey) with pass line 75.
lines: Your idea: instead of a small add-on, let sleep nudge every part of the brain, just a tiny bit.
The worry was that squeezing would round those tiny nudges away. It didn't. About ninety-four percent of the gain survived. The pass mark was seventy-five.
A bigger, three-week test is designed and waiting.

title: Skill sleep
visual: A shop counter with tool icons. Bars on K2 (teal): no sleep 63.8, learning from good and bad tries 66.9, pass line 69.8. A small label 'not significant'.
lines: Skill sleep tries to learn skills, like using tools in a fake online shop, from good tries and bad ones.
On K2 it went up about three points. That's too small to count. It needed six.
Next time, it gets four times more practice.

title: Ask once, then remember
visual: Speech bubble 'Which Sam?' then a notebook entry 'Sam = Sam Lee' then next time the assistant acts with a check mark. A stamp 'first run stopped on day 1'.
lines: Ask once, then remember teaches the assistant when to ask you a question, and when to just get on with it. Then it remembers your answer.
Its first run stopped on day one, because the model's replies couldn't be read. So there's no score yet.

title: Diary memory
visual: A diary with every chat stored word for word and a magnifying glass. Bars (amber, 'Claude stand-in'): search raw chats 71.7, written notes 56.7.
lines: During the day, the assistant keeps every chat word for word, in a diary it can search. Like scrolling back through old texts.
We tested writing tidy notes instead. Searching the raw chats won, seventy-two to fifty-seven.

title: Thinking loop
visual: Question -> a circular loop with lap arrows -> answer. Bars (grey): loop 67.0, plain extra practice 70.8, pass line 74.6.
lines: The thinking loop lets the model go round and round silently before answering, like re-reading your scratch work.
So far, it hasn't helped. It scored sixty-seven. Plain extra practice scored seventy-one. And adding more laps changed nothing.
There's one last try running on your PC. If it misses, we drop it.

title: Creative mode
visual: Many guess cards fan out, a checker with a magnifying glass, one card gets a green tick. Bar (grey): puzzles right 67.6 with label '97.7% precision', vs v1 34.8. Then four small cards stamped 'not run yet'.
lines: When it's stuck, creative mode throws out lots of guesses, and a checker keeps only the ones that really work.
On puzzles, it doubled what version one could do. But it missed its harder targets.
Four new versions, built for real assistant tasks, are ready but haven't run yet.

title: Multi-step puzzles
visual: A rising staircase (grey): 2 nights 10.2, 4 nights 16.9, 8 nights 26.0. Next to it three crossed-out trick cards: 'dream school', 'hindsight', 'chained programs'.
lines: Some puzzles take three to five steps to solve.
The only thing that worked was more nights of sleep. Hard puzzles went from ten to twenty-six. Every other trick we tried, failed.

title: Leapfrog
visual: Two climbers taking turns going ahead on a mountain. A line chart (grey) by round: 12.5, 20.8, 21.7, 21.8, 22.0, 22.7. A label 'the real leapfrog never ran'.
lines: Leapfrog was your idea. The explorer climbs ahead, the worker sleeps on what it found, and they take turns.
Only the warm-up ran. It jumped after night one, then went flat. It's on the shelf for now.

title: Dopamine
visual: A spark labelled 'surprise = reward minus what you expected'. Bars (grey): plain reward 27, surprise signal 21, pass line 32. A small wrench icon crossed out: 'learned to skip its tools'.
lines: Dopamine was about learning harder from surprises, like your brain does.
It made things worse. Twenty-one, against twenty-seven without it. It learned a shortcut: skipping its tools.
So the nightly lessons now use your corrections instead. This answer, not that one.

title: Claude grader
visual: A teacher (Claude) marking tries with A/B/C grades. Bars (grey): before 25, after round 1 25, pass line 35. Speech bubble 'I sent the email!' with no email sent.
lines: Here, Claude grades each try, like a teacher, and the model trains toward better grades.
Round one gave no gain. The model learned to say it had done things, without actually doing them.
Round two closes that loophole. It's running now.

title: Backbones and speed
visual: Two laptops: big laptop with 'Qwen3.6-35B' (violet), small laptop with 'K2-3.7B' (teal). Bars: speed per agent with 2 agents at once: Qwen 30, K2 30 tokens/sec, pass line 30.
lines: Everything sits on a borrowed brain. Qwen for big laptops, K2 for small ones.

Your goal is several helpers at once, each writing at least thirty tokens a second. A token is a small piece of a word. With two helpers running, both hit thirty, right on the line. With four, they slow down. That's next to fix.

title: What's next
visual: The index page summary: 6 Adopted, 6 Testing, 3 Refuted, 1 Parked. Then a calendar 'Ben's Week: 10 fake weeks of real-life tasks, last 3 sealed'. Ending on the laptop with the glowing brain and a moon.
lines: So that's the map.
Sleep works, and it works on both real brains. The big open questions are two-step memory, skills, and whether thinking loops can pay off.
And the final exam is waiting: Ben's Week. Ten weeks of pretend school life, with the last three sealed, for the finished assistant.
Thanks for watching.
